messages.author: 6fbf4419e048b767
messages.subject: Polytomous Item Response Theory
parts:
Dear Stan users,

I just started to use Stan to fit polytomous item response theory models.
The model file is attached below.
I used a BUGS-like style to write the model. But it doesn't seem to work. 
Y[n, j] is the data point that follows categorical distribution. But it seems like Stan didn't recognize the probability vector prob[n, j, 1:C].
Any idea on how to define the probability vector would be appreciated.
Also, the normal_cdf( ) doesn't seem to be the best way to define the prob[ ], any suggestion on that?
Not sure if the chain will run fast enough with my current parameterization.

Best,
Yao

data {
  int N;                         // number of assignment being rated
  int J;                         // number of raters
  int C;                         // number of rating categories
  int<lower=1, upper=C> Y[N, J]; // rating data matrix
}


parameters {    
  real theta[N];               // assignment true score
  real delta[J];               // rater sys bias
  real a[J];                   // rater discrimination
  ordered[C-1] gamma;          // threshold
  real<lower=0> tau[J];        // rater precision parameter
}


model {
  real sigma[J];
  real prob[N, J, C];
  theta ~ normal(0, 1);
  delta ~ normal(0, 2);
  a ~ lognormal(0, 0.5);
  gamma ~ normal(0, 2);
  tau ~ gamma(1, 1);
  for (j in 1:J)
  sigma[j] <- pow(tau[j], -0.5);
 
  for (n in 1:N) {
     for (j in 1:J) {
      for (c in 2:(C-1)) {
      prob[n, j, c] <- normal_cdf((gamma[c]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]) - normal_cdf((gamma[c-1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]); }
      prob[n, j, 1] <- normal_cdf((gamma[1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]);
      prob[n, j, C] <- 1 - sum(prob[n, j, 1:4]);
      Y[n, j] ~ categorical(prob[n, j, 1:C]);   // here is the bug
     }
  }
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Polytomous Item Response Theory
parts:
I'd suggest taking a look at some of the Stan models in
the manual. We won't be supporting the BUGS/JAGS a:b
slicing notation for matrices/arrays until Stan 2.9.0,
and it's still not worked through our examples.

Instead, you can use prob[n, j] instead of prob[n, j, 1:C]
if the last dimension is size C. Otherwise, you have
to slice it somehow manually.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Polytomous Item Response Theory
parts: See below.

> On Jan 7, 2016, at 10:04 AM, Yao Xiong <xy.xi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> No matches for:
>
>
> int ~ categorical(real[])
>
>
> Available argument signatures for categorical:
>
>
> int ~ categorical(vector)
> int[] ~ categorical(vector)
>
>
>
>
> ERROR at line 33
>
>
> 31: prob[n, j, 1] <- normal_cdf((gamma[1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]);
> 32: prob[n, j, C] <- 1 - sum(prob[n, j, 1:4]);

> 33: Y[n, j] ~ categorical(prob[n, j]);
> ^

The error messages says you used:

> int ~ categorical(real[])

That is, Y[n, j] is an int and prob[n, j] is an *array* of reals.

You can then see that the available argument signatures are:

> int ~ categorical(vector)
> int[] ~ categorical(vector)

So the mismatch is that you've provided a real[] argument (array
of reals) and the multivariate distributions all require *vector* parameters.

There's an entire chapter of the manual near the front devoted
to arrays vs. vectors and their usage in Stan. Hint: It's more like
MATLAB than R or BUGS.

Rather than to_vector, which does copying, you want to read the
chapter of the Stan manual on arrays, so you'll understand why I'm
about to suggest that you declare prob as

vector[C] prob[N, J];

an N x J array of C-vectors, rather than as an N x J x C array.

But that's still a holdover from BUGS style. Stan has local variables,
so you should just declare

vector[C] prob;

and define that in the loop. But your code there isn't wrong so
much as suboptimally coded (it would have been wrong in BUGS):

for (n in 1:N) {
> for (j in 1:J) {
> for (c in 2:(C-1)) {
> prob[n, j, c] <- normal_cdf((gamma[c]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]) - normal_cdf((gamma[c-1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]); }
> prob[n, j, 1] <- normal_cdf((gamma[1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]);
> prob[n, j, C] <- 1 - sum(prob[n, j, 1:4]);
> Y[n, j] ~ categorical(prob[n, j, 1:C]); // here is the bug
> }
> }
> }

You want to define prob[1] and prob[C] outside of the loop for C.

But if you're just trying to code up an ordinal logit, we have that
built in.

- Bob

>       for (c in 2:(C-1)) {
>       prob[n, j, c] <- normal_cdf((gamma[c]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]) - normal_cdf((gamma[c-1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]); }

You want to define prob[1] and prob[C] outside of the loop for C.

built in.

- Bob

> On Jan 7, 2016, at 12:14 PM, Yao Xiong <xy.xi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks so much, Bob.
> I actually did changed the parameter to vector[C] prob[N, J], and the chain did run.
> But I am aware that the code is not optimal, still working on how to make it better.
> You are right that there isn't parallel function in BUGS as normal_cdf( ) in Stan. But in JAGS, there is pnorm( ).
> As you suggested, if I define vector[C] prob, does that mean prob is a NxJ matrix?

No! It means it's a C-vector. But that's all you need. It's
a local variable and can get redefined in each loop iteration.
Much more efficient than allocating a huge array and filling it
and then just throwing it away.

> I do need different values for each n and j combination for prob.
> The reason I didn't use the ordered_logistic( ) is because I wanted to add the parameter sigma[j], so there are heterogenous variances for different j.

All you need is the linear predictor and cutpoints and it'll do
all that munging of the CDFs for you. It looks like you're using
probit, but logit is much much faster to compute and gives almost
identical (albeit differently scaled) results.

- Bob
